Date: 2026-10-15
Time: 14:00 - 14:56 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Sara Liu (BluePeak CTO), Mark Hernandez (BluePeak Lead ML Eng), Priya Nair (BluePeak Infra Eng), Ethan Cole (BluePeak SRE)
summary: Deep dive on KV-cache eviction, paging and prefix reuse patterns. Discussed cache sizing, tail latencies on long-context sessions, interactions with batching and quantization, and constraints for BluePeak's VPC deployment. Agreed next steps: pilot with BluePeak traffic, log collection, and follow-up benchmark call.
topics: VPC/on-prem constraints and network egress/ingress for cache state
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you squeezing this in, we wanted to focus on your KV-cache symptoms and figure out root causes, also go over mitigation patterns.
[00:08] Sara Liu: Thanks, Maya. Quick intro - I'm Sara, CTO at BluePeak, we've been seeing occasional token-level regressions and some tail latency spikes when users hit long sessions, especially for multi-turn financial compliance conversations.
[00:20] Mark Hernandez: Yeah, hi, Mark here. We run about 80% of traffic on long-context flows, a mix of 8k and occasional 32k windows, and we suspect the cache is getting evicted mid-conversation which forces re-rolls.
[00:33] Jonas Reed: Got it. Quick clarifying q - when you say evicted, do you mean full KV pages being paged out due to memory pressure or prefix-level eviction because of misaligned tokenization? Two different patterns.
[00:44] Priya Nair: We're not 100% sure. What we observe is a sudden increase in token generation time and sometimes repeated prefixes re-sent, looks like cold-cache rehydration.
[00:54] Maya Patel: Also, we noted you use a private VPC deployment with a dedicated Redwood node pool, correct? There might be config differences in page size or memory cap.
[01:04] Ethan Cole: Correct, it's a VPC deployment with constrained GPU memory budget, we applied the default cache size but didn't tune for our 32k workflows.
[01:12] Jonas Reed: Cool. So broad causes: 1) cache footprint exceeds configured KV capacity causing LRU-style eviction; 2) prefix reuse mismatch - if tokenization differs across clients, similar-looking prompts map to different prefixes; 3) paging - when KV cache is too big we page chunks to host memory and that adds latency; 4) quantization-related recomputation overhead.
[01:30] Mark Hernandez: We suspected quantization would be unrelated, but you're saying it can affect cache behavior?
[01:36] Jonas Reed: Indirectly. If model variants differ by quantization level, kernel selection and decoder throughput changes, which can change lifetime of KV entries in memory and how batching aggregates requests. Also tiny differences in tokenization across model variants can break prefix reuse.
[01:50] Sara Liu: Hmm, we do have mixed model variants during fallbacks - sometimes we route to a 4-bit quantised variant for cost.
[01:58] Jonas Reed: That explains some of the 'cold' reads. When we fallback to a quantized variant that uses a different tokenizer or has different prefix normalization, the cached KV keys won't match.
[02:07] Lena Ortiz: One note - Redwood's default is to keep separate KV namespaces per model-version by default to avoid cross-variant pollution, but you can enable shared namespace with careful normalization.
[02:19] Priya Nair: Can you explain paging more? We're seeing spikes where latency jumps from 120ms to 900ms for a few tokens.
[02:26] Jonas Reed: Sure. Paging happens when the per-GPU usable KV RAM is exhausted and the runtime moves older KV shards to host memory or NVMe. The first token after a page-in suffers the round-trip to host and back, which is the big spike. If your request distribution is skewed, you'll page hot prefixes back in frequently.
[02:44] Maya Patel: This is where heatmaps help - we usually ask customers to provide per-prefix frequency and session-length distribution so we can estimate resident working set.
[02:52] Mark Hernandez: We can get top-100 prefixes but 32k context means prefixes can be many more.
[02:58] Jonas Reed: Right, top-K prefixes gives a lot of signal; also sample tail sessions. For long-context multi-turn flows, the working set is roughly the sum of unique prefixes plus their KV expansion.
[03:10] Ethan Cole: What about batching? We batch for throughput but it appears batching sometimes increases tail latency because a batch waits for slow sessions.
[03:18] Jonas Reed: Good point. There is a classic tradeoff: larger batch windows increase throughput and amortize KV loads but add queueing latency. For long-context sessions with intermittent activity, adaptive batching or per-route low-latency lanes works well - keep a small batch cap for your interactive flows.
[03:33] Sara Liu: We have a hybrid traffic mix - can you recommend heuristics?
[03:36] Jonas Reed: Set two policies: interactive (max batch 4 tokens or 8ms max wait) and background (larger batch). Also enable prefix-level caching for repeated system messages and normalize white-space/tokens to maximize reuse.
[03:48] Mark Hernandez: About normalization - we use client-side templating that sometimes injects timestamps and user IDs, so identical semantics don't map to identical prefixes. Any best practice?
[03:57] Jonas Reed: Strip ephemeral fields server-side before tokenizing for cache keys, or use hashed placeholders. Redwood has a plugin to canonicalize templates before caching. That greatly improves prefix reuse.
[04:07] Maya Patel: Another angle is eviction policy - LRU is default, but for sessions we sometimes prefer session-aware retention where active sessions pin KV blocks. Would that help?
[04:16] Jonas Reed: Yes. Session pinning is effective: you mark session KV as high priority and use a capped pinned pool to avoid starvation. The trick is you need to estimate session lifetime and cap pinned footprint to avoid displacing frequently reused prefixes.
[04:28] Priya Nair: For our workflows, sessions last up to 90 minutes, some are idle and resume. Pinning might keep memory stressed.
[04:36] Jonas Reed: Then a hybrid - pin the latest N turns rather than entire session; or use TTL-based pinning where pins decay after X idle seconds.
[04:45] Sara Liu: You mentioned prefix reuse problems from tokenization differences earlier - how often is that mis-tokenization causing eviction?
[04:51] Jonas Reed: It can be surprisingly common. Even whitespace variance or unicode punctuation can create distinct keys. For high-cardinality prefixes you get poor reuse and an inflated working set which causes evictions.
[05:03] Mark Hernandez: Ok, practical diagnostics - what logs/metrics should we collect?
[05:07] Jonas Reed: Collect per-token latency histograms, per-prefix cache hit/miss counts, page-in/page-out events with timestamps, batch sizes distribution, model-variant per-request, and memory pressure metrics per GPU. We'll provide a diagnostic script.
[05:21] Maya Patel: Jonas, can you call out threshold numbers we should be looking at for page-in rate that indicate under-provisioning?
[05:28] Jonas Reed: If page-in events exceed, say, 1% of token requests during steady-state for an interactive workflow, you're likely under-provisioned. Also watch for repeated page-in for the same prefix within short windows - that's the smoking gun.
[05:40] Priya Nair: We're seeing page-in about 2.5% during peak hours.
[05:44] Jonas Reed: That's consistent with the spikes you're seeing. Two levers: increase KV memory per GPU or reduce working set via normalization/pinning; or add more GPUs with sharded KV so working set spreads.
[05:56] Ethan Cole: What about slow NVMe - we run on cloud instances with networked NVMe. Page-in penalties are sometimes worse.
[06:02] Jonas Reed: NVMe latency matters a lot. On-prem with local NVMe or host RAM fallback is better. For cloud, prefer instances with local NVMe, or add a caching tier for the hottest pages in RAM.
[06:12] Sara Liu: Any impact from model quantization on KV index size?
[06:16] Jonas Reed: Quantization usually reduces model weight sizes but KV cache entries are mostly activations and key/value vectors - quantization can reduce KV size if you store compressed activations, but some optimizations avoid quantizing KV embeddings to preserve quality. If you do compress KV by 4-bit, you reduce RAM pressure but add decompression cost on access which can add latency.
[06:33] Mark Hernandez: So it's a tradeoff again.
[06:35] Jonas Reed: Exactly. For latency-sensitive flows we keep KV uncompressed; for background batch jobs we can compress. Redwood has per-route KV storage policies.
[06:44] Maya Patel: Let's talk prefix reuse and tokenization disambiguation briefly - any examples?
[06:49] Jonas Reed: Sure. Example: two system prompts differ only by a generated timestamp - naive tokenization creates two keys. If you canonicalize to replace timestamps with <TS>, cached KV hits multiply. Another example: different punctuation (smart quotes vs straight quotes) tokenize differently; normalize unicode.
[07:06] Priya Nair: We'll need help rolling canonicalization in our client.
[07:09] Jonas Reed: We'll share a small client-side normalization library and server-side hook.
[07:13] Lena Ortiz: Also note that for Private deployments, some customers prefer to do normalization in their VPC to avoid sending preprocessed payloads out; we support that pattern.
[07:23] Sara Liu: Re: VPC constraints, is there any limitation for page-in/out between GPU and host in VPC?
[07:29] Jonas Reed: Functionally nothing different, but network configs and cgroup memory limits you set on the instance can make page-in worse. Also if you're using mounted network storage for NVMe, that adds additional latency.
[07:40] Ethan Cole: Is there telemetry Redwood can collect from our VPC deployment or is it all customer-side?
[07:45] Maya Patel: We can collect anonymized diagnostics if you allow it; for enterprise Private deployments we usually run an agent in the VPC that only transmits metrics and not PII or prompts. It's part of the pilot setup.
[07:57] Mark Hernandez: Cool. About benchmark - what should we run for the follow-up?
[08:00] Jonas Reed: Run a two-stage benchmark: 1) steady-state long-session replay of top-1k prefixes at production concurrency; 2) stress test with randomized long-context sessions to exercise paging. Measure token latency p50/p95/p99, page-in rate, cache hit ratio, batch size distribution, and model variant switch frequency.
[08:18] Sara Liu: We'll need a template for replay harness.
[08:21] Jonas Reed: We'll share the harness and a config that mimics your traffic.
[08:24] Maya Patel: Quick callout on rollout best practices - when you change cache config or model variant, do canary first with a small percent of traffic and explicitly monitor page-in rate.
[08:33] Mark Hernandez: Noted.
[08:35] Priya Nair: Any immediate low-effort mitigations we can apply?
[08:38] Jonas Reed: Yes: 1) deploy normalization plugin to reduce distinct prefixes; 2) pin most recent 4 turns per active session with TTL; 3) set a small interactive batch cap; 4) for quantized fallbacks, align tokenizers or avoid switching variants mid-session. These usually reduce page-in and tail latency quickly.
[08:56] Sara Liu: Sounds good. One more question - do you have any guidance for telemetry retention and privacy for PCI-related data?
[09:02] Maya Patel: We avoid storing raw prompts in telemetry. For PCI scope, we only collect hashed keys and metrics; for pilot we can mask PII client-side. We'll include the security docs.
[09:12] Sara Liu: Great.
[09:14] Jonas Reed: I'll follow up with the eviction diagnostic script and the normalization plugin.
[09:18] Maya Patel: Ok let's recap next steps - pilot, logs, follow-up benchmark call, and security/pricing.
[09:24] Sara Liu: Agreed. Thanks everyone.
[09:26] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll send notes and action items.
[09:30] [call ends]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker overlap, some technical terms mistranscribed (e.g., 'quantised' vs 'quantized', NVMe noted as NVM-e in one snippet).
